items.title: Challenge To Mamdani's Rent Freeze Thrown Out By Judge
items.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani 's historic rent freeze will stay in place after a judge dismissed a lawsuit Wednesday from a group of landlords. Flickr/Mayoral Photography Office/Ed Reed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani After the New York City Rent Guidelines Board voted in June to freeze rents on one- and two-year leases across the city's 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, landlords represented by Randy Mastro, first deputy mayor under Eric Adams, filed a lawsuit alleging the decision was a result of a “sham process.” But in a decision issued Wednesday morning, New York County Supreme Court Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed the lawsuit, finding that the RGB's decision had “a rational basis,” and therefore the courts had no ability to reverse it. The freeze already went into effect Oct. 1, the first time in the RGB's 57-year history that rents on both one- and two-year leases were barred from being raised. Mamdani campaigned last year on freezing the rent for all four years in office and appointed a majority of the RGB, but the board is supposed to independently make its decision, informed by data, market conditions and public testimony. “When this lawsuit was filed, the Law Department made clear that the board had acted within its authority and that tenants needed this relief,” Mamdani said in a statement. “Today, Judge Lantry affirmed what we knew all along: the Rent Guidelines Board had the authority to deliver for the more than two million New Yorkers who call rent-stabilized apartments home.” A group of landlords that own apartment buildings in Staten Island and Queens, the plaintiffs going after the city, claimed the RGB ignored its own data that showed expenses have skyrocketed for property owners and many were underwater on their mortgages. Some of the landlords are members of the Small Property Owners of New York , which called the dismissal “terribly disappointing.” Owners of rent-stabilized units are dealing with insurance, maintenance and operating costs that have soared in recent years, and they can’t boost their revenue to compensate for higher expenses. “We were hopeful the court would have recognized that the RGB blatantly ignored its own data, which clearly signaled a rent increase, and instead capitulated to the political pressures of City Hall to ensure that Mayor Mamdani made good on his rent freeze campaign promise,” SPONY Board President Ann Korchak said in a statement. “The rent freeze will push more small rent-stabilized property owners to the edge of the cliff.” The landlords allege that Mamdani's administration pressured the RGB into its decision, and they sought to uncover communications between City Hall and board members. More than 1,000 emails and text messages were released as part of the discovery process in the suit, showing frequent outreach from the administration . But after the sides agreed to halt discovery last month, Lantry wrote in his decision that not enough evidence was presented to suggest the city illegally influenced the RGB. But he admonished the new mayor for his campaign vow and the perception it created. “Such comments, promises, and guarantees to freeze the rent were reckless and irresponsible,” the judge wrote. “The Mayor of the City of New York has no authority to unilaterally raise, ‘freeze’ or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this City — that responsibility is within the power of the Board and the Board alone.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Ann Korchak , NYC Rent Guidelines Board , Randy Mastro , Rent Freeze , Rent Guidelines Board , Rent Stabilization , Rent stabilized apartments , Small Property Owners of New York , Zohran Mamdani

items.title: From Mold Poisoning to Lyme Disease: Inside the Extreme Moves 6 Stars Made to Save Their Health
items.description: In many cases, a health diagnosis can be life-changing. From dealing with symptoms to navigating treatment, managing medical issues is no easy feat. And while accessibility upgrades and wellness integrations can certainly make a home more habitable in these instances, some people choose to pack up and move altogether—particularly celebrities. Because their diagnoses may be complicated by the nuances that come along with fame and being in the public eye , it’s no surprise that some celebs may choose to find a home with more privacy when faced with health challenges. Of course, celebrities may also have the means to relocate when particular symptoms could be managed more easily in a different climate. Although some high profile individuals prefer to keep these kinds of decisions close to the chest, a handful of celebs have spoken candidly about the health-related circumstances that inspired them to migrate. Jenny McCarthy considers Las Vegas to escape humidity Loading... Jenny McCarthy revealed she is planning to move to Las Vegas or Arizona in pursuit of a dry climate as she deals with mold and mycotoxin poisoning. YouTube/The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show Loading... The actress is currently residing in a tent in her yard as she deals with symptoms. YouTube/The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg recently offloaded their longtime Illinois residence for $2.6 million. The transaction comes just as “The Masked Singer” host has publicly shared her experience dealing with the effects of “mold and mycotoxin poisoning.” During the Oct. 28 episode of “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” she revealed that she’s been living in a tent after undergoing the costly experience of remediating her home . In a later episode, McCarthy also noted that she has discarded all of her clothing and furniture in a continued attempt to escape the mold. In the wake of the ordeal, she’s considering a relocation. “I’m so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donny about moving out of the midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” McCarthy said. McCarthy and Wahlberg have yet to make a permanent move, but the sale of their St. Charles property could certainly be the first step towards change. Matt Holliday leaves dream home in Oklahoma for dry climate Loading... Retired MLB player Matt Holliday was diagnosed with a respiratory disease, with his doctor encouraging him to flee to a dryer climate. MLB Photos via Getty Images Loading... Holliday and his wife left their Oklahoma dream home to relocate to Arizona. They're now selling the Paradise Valley home they initially moved to. Rocket Lister Retired Major League Baseball star Matt Holliday and his wife, Leslie Holliday , were left with no choice but to leave the dream home they’d built in Stillwater, OK , when he was diagnosed with a respiratory disease. “The doctor said he needed to get to dry climate quick,” listing agent Vincent Clark told the Phoenix Business Journal . Clark is the agent representing the sale of the Paradise Valley, AZ property the Hollidays initially relocated to. They purchased the $10.6 million home in February of this year after the World Series champion received the diagnosis a week after a water leak had affected their 136-acre custom home in Oklahoma , which is still on the market for $8.95 million. While the sprawling Arizona property was well-equipped with “substantial healthy-home enhancements” including air and water filtration and conditioning systems, Clark revealed that the Hollidays are seeking a home with an existing guest house, although the 7,781-square-foot home they’re hoping to sell includes transferred approved plans for an 845-square-foot guest casita. Mikayla Matthews builds a new home in Utah Loading... Mikayla Matthews has been dealing with Chronic Inflammatory Response Syndrome, which she believes is a result of mold in her home. JC Olivera/Variety via Getty Images Loading... The reality star has temporarily relocated to Hawaii and Florida, but is now building a new home in Utah. TikTok In an Aug.10 social media post, “ The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives ” alum Mikayla Matthews admitted that her “home situation is always up in the air.” The reality TV personality was diagnosed with Chronic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (CIRS), which she believes was triggered by extended exposure to mold-related toxins. She and her family spent much of 2026 traveling in hopes of easing her symptoms, and temporarily relocated to Hawaii in May before heading to Florida in June in pursuit of a humid climate. “The heavy metals in the air from Great Salt Lake drying up add to my toxic load everyday, so I can’t detox everything out,” she wrote in an Instagram post. In October, Matthews revealed that her family was leaving the home she says was “making” her “sick,” and had purchased a new home in Utah , which is still under construction. Bella Hadid snaps up space in Texas Loading... Bella Hadid stepped back from modeling in 2024, citing a struggle with mental health and Lyme disease. Neilson Barnard/Getty Images Loading... She purchased a home in Fort Worth, TX, and began to focus on horseback riding instead. Bella Hadid/Instagram Bella Hadid recently purchased an idyllic $5.5 million home in Colorado , but it’s not the first time she’s snapped up a property with a stunning connection to nature. In 2024, the model spoke to Allure about her decision to take a break from the industry in pursuit of a more laid back lifestyle in Fort Worth, TX , citing mental health struggles including severe anxiety and brain fog, as well as her longtime battle with Lyme disease. The move marked a focus on her mental and physical health, as well as a dedication to a passion she’d lost with fame: horseback riding. items.title: Court upholds NYC rent freeze backed by Mayor Mamdani
items.description: On Thanksgiving eve, Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a landlords' challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board's late June decision to freeze rents. The ruling upholds the city's first-ever freeze on both one- and two-year leases. With the national real estate industry watching, the rent freeze became a major test of what a mayor can do to force affordability. Owners of rent-stabilized buildings argued that Mamdani stacked the board with loyalists after promising a freeze, making the outcome predetermined. They also accused the board of following a campaign promise instead of the data on rising landlord costs. Lantry rejected both claims. The ruling comes three weeks after an appeals court revived the city's pied-à-terre tax rollout on second homes valued at $5 million or higher. Mamdani posted on social media that the city has billed owners of those homes more than $500 million. That lawsuit ran parallel to the rent freeze lawsuit landlords filed in late July. It originally was in a Staten Island court but was moved to Manhattan in August at the city's request. The rent freeze took effect Oct. 1 while the lawsuit was pending and covers leases on more than a million apartments. The board had frozen one-year leases in 2015, 2016 and 2020. Because the board acts in a quasi-legislative role, its orders stand if they have a rational basis, and courts may not substitute their own judgment, Lantry wrote. He found that the board's 42-page explanatory statement showed it considered each factor the Administrative Code requires, including the industry's economic condition and the cost of living. Lantry said appointees who share the mayor's views did not show collusion. He noted that "elections have consequences." Ruling comes with criticism But Lantry did not let Mamdani completely off the hook. "Regarding Mayor Mamdani's campaign for Mayor of New York City, the court would be remiss not to state that such comments, promises, and guarantees to freeze the rent were reckless and irresponsible," he wrote. "The Mayor of the City of New York has no authority to unilaterally raise, 'freeze' or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this City – that responsibility is within the power of the Board and the Board alone." He called an email in which the board's chair shared a draft of the explanatory statement with a mayoral aide before the vote "troubling." He said it cast a "dark shadow" over the board's independence. Without more, he wrote, the email did not justify overturning the decision under Article 78, the state law that lets courts review government agency actions. The judge noted that petitioners agreed to end court-ordered discovery, which produced about 1,000 documents, and never sought depositions. Lantry acknowledged the freeze could make it harder for owners to refinance or renovate. But he wrote that the legal question is not whether the policy is wise. Related More: Affordability New York City Rent Prices

items.title: Google Buys King's Cross HQ For £500M: The London Deal Sheet
items.description: The Deal Sheet is a weekly compilation of Greater London and beyond's biggest leases, sales, financing deals, construction updates and personnel moves. Have news you'd like to submit? Email mark.faithfull@bisnow.com . BNP Paribas Asset Management Alts and Canadian pension investor PSP Investments are to sell 6 Pancras Square in King's Cross to its occupier, Google, in a £500M deal that will see the investors exit one of their longest-held London office investments. The joint venture acquired the 371K SF, Grade A office building in 2013 through a development forward-funding arrangement, and the property includes 32K SF of retail space across six units. Courtesy of BNPP AM Alts and PSP Investments/Edmund Summer Google is to acquire its headquarters in a deal affirming UK ambitions. BNP Paribas AM Alts, formerly AXA IM Alts, managed the joint venture on behalf of investors including PSP Investments. Google UK and Ireland Managing Director and Vice President Kate Alessi said the purchase underlined the company's long-term commitment to the UK. “Our purchase of 6 Pancras Square sends a clear signal of our long-term commitment to the UK. This investment ensures our UK teams can continue building world-changing AI, driving innovation, and contributing to the growth of the country's economy,” Alessi said in a statement. DEALS London Square has acquired the Boord Street development on Greenwich Peninsula from Fairview New Homes and will deliver all 352 homes as affordable housing through its registered provider, Square Roots. The development has detailed planning permission for three buildings ranging from eight to 25 storeys. The site has been cleared, enabling works have been undertaken, and Building Safety Regulator Gateway 2 approval has been secured, allowing construction to start immediately. Completion is expected in June 2029. The conversion of the previously private-led development into 100% affordable housing has been supported by an £87M grant allocation from the mayor of London. The homes will comprise 80% social rent and 20% intermediate rent, with Greenwich Council making nominations for the social rent properties. *** The Hill Group and Principal Asset Management have agreed a £27.3M transaction for 67 build-to-rent apartments at Canalside Quarter, the first residential phase of the £700M Oxford North master plan. The apartments, comprising one-to-three-bedroom homes, will provide managed rental accommodation within the mixed-use development, which is bringing together residential, research and laboratory space, offices, retail, community facilities and public parks. “This transaction is another important milestone in the growth of Hill's Build-to-Rent platform and demonstrates the increasing confidence institutional investors have in our ability to create high-quality rental homes within thriving mixed-tenure communities,” Hill Senior Asset Manager Tom Starkey said in a statement. *** Savills Investment Management's Simply Affordable Homes fund has acquired 288 affordable homes at Whitstable Heights in Kent from Hyde Housing Association. The purchase, its fourth acquisition, was made through the fund's for-profit registered provider, Simply Affordable Homes RP. The portfolio comprises 204 houses and 84 apartments across social rent, affordable rent and shared ownership tenures and represents the majority of the 400-home development, which was delivered by Hyde in partnership with Chartway Partnerships Group and completed in 2026. The fund now manages more than 700 affordable rent, intermediate rent and shared ownership homes across southern England, the east of England and the Midlands. DEVELOPMENT Developer Hub and Norwegian investor Smedvig have submitted revised plans for the final phase of their One Maidenhead master plan, with proposals for an eight-storey, 70K SF office building. The scheme, named Arven, will sit next to Maidenhead station, between the transport hub and town centre. It will include ground-floor retail and café space, two roof terraces, and additional office and external amenity space. The revised design builds on an existing planning permission, adding a red brick facade to complement the residential buildings and targeting BREEAM Excellent. The first phase of One Maidenhead, completed in 2024, delivered 429 rental homes, 36K SF of retail and restaurant space, and a new public garden. Construction of neighbouring office building Trehus is nearing completion. *** Barratt London and Transport for London property company Places for London have named Ickenham Gardens as the latest site for their West London Partnership joint venture. The site, between Ickenham and Ruislip Gardens, has the potential to deliver around 2,000 homes, half of which would be affordable, alongside improved public green spaces, transport connections and community facilities. The emerging plans will seek to create a new neighbourhood between two established communities, with a mix of home sizes, types and tenures. The proposals also include opportunities for health, education, cultural and community facilities. FINANCE Private credit manager Evermill Capital, backed by Delancey, has launched an infrastructure credit strategy, extending its existing real estate lending platform into infrastructure finance. Evermill has already committed more than £100M to cash-flow-matching infrastructure investments as it develops the new strategy. The business has appointed Tim Floyd as a partner to lead the expansion. He joins from Westbourne Capital, where he spent 13 years building its European infrastructure credit business and deploying more than £3B for insurers, pension funds and sovereign wealth funds. items.title: Florida Slashed Homestead Taxes. Commercial Real Estate Could Pay The Price
items.description: The Florida commercial real estate industry is holding its collective breath — and hitting pause on some deals — as cities and counties grapple with a new state law that will slash their budgets by millions. Unsplash/Zoshua Colah Miami City Hall at 3500 Pan American Drive Amendment 3, approved on Election Day by 62% of Florida voters, raises the state’s homestead exemption, which only applies to permanent residences, from $50K to $150K next year and $250K in 2028. Set to go into effect by Jan. 1, the law doesn't include tax levies for school district properties. While the new law was passed on the promise of affordability, its impact is prompting local authorities to weigh service reductions, spending freezes, increased fees, and tax rate adjustments that would ultimately leave the private sector to fill the gap. “Our biggest concern, and it applies across the board and all our expenses, is uncertainty,” said Rick Porras, chief financial officer of multifamily developer Neology. “We need to know what playing field we're going to be dealing with.” Gov. Ron DeSantis campaigned on slashing property taxes last year as a way to lower housing costs for homeowners in Florida, where the cost of living index is nearly 2% above the national benchmark, according to a third-quarter Missouri Economic Research and Information Center report . The affordability crisis is more acute in South Florida, where Miami’s cost of living has surpassed that of New York and where more than 50% of Miami-Dade County households are living paycheck to paycheck, the Miami Herald reported . Property taxes account for 43% of municipal general fund revenue, according to a Florida League of Cities study conducted by Wichita State University. Losing a large chunk of that poses a significant risk to local budgets, especially those with smaller commercial real estate tax bases and higher debt levels. Local governments are projected to lose nearly $5B of funding in the next fiscal year, CBS News reported . In response, cities all over the state are canceling Christmas parades , ending funding for transportation services and eyeing hiring freezes and spending cuts . “There are cities that do not have the commercial tax base that would help them offset some of the loss in revenue,” Porras said. “If the cities are heavily dependent on residential properties, they're going to suffer even more than others.” But even cities with a large commercial base are expecting to take a hit, especially to public services. Miami Mayor Eileen Higgins said at Bisnow’s Condoverse conference in April that the city was prepping a 25% budget cut , which would hit city services like local hospitals, police, fire, parks, public schools and water management. Her office didn't respond to a request for comment for this story. Billionaire developer and “ Condo King of Miami ” Jorge Pérez warned such moves could threaten Miami’s ability to attract and retain residents. Some municipalities are considering raising millage rates, or taxing a higher percentage of a property's value. Not only could a higher millage rate cut into the savings homeowners would get with Amendment 3, but commercial owners would face the same higher rate without an exemption to help offset it. Fort Lauderdale Mayor Dean Trantalis told Bisnow the week the amendment passed that he was “very real about raising” his city's millage rates and that he will lean on the community, which will make a decision on “whether they want to increase taxes or reduce services.” “[You] can’t have the same level of service you have come to expect over the years,” he said. “Cities are going to have to deal with it,” he added. “That was a bad choice, but now we have to live with that.” Palm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo told 25 WPBG News in September there were three options for the county to help offset a hit to the budget: cut the budget, significantly affecting first responders and county departments; raise the millage rate; or a combination of both. Assuming there is no taxable value growth, South Florida counties would need to raise their millage rates more than 10% per county to collect the equivalent quantity of tax and keep budgets the same, according to a white paper written by Nick Mau, partner at property tax advisory firm FirstPoint Advisors LLC. A raise in millage rates would likely trickle down to commercial tenants, especially on leases where tenants pay property taxes separately from rent, said Melissa Tapanes Llahues, a land use and zoning attorney and CEO of Bercow Radell Fernandez Larkin and Tapanes. Unsplash/Martley U The Fort Lauderdale skyline While Florida bars municipalities from raising fees on services to generate revenue, a rising concern for the development community is that local governments expand their powers to require greater public improvements and the payment of impact fees, she said. The new law could affect what localities will want developers to build, she added. "I think that government will be more open, welcoming, and incentivize commercial and industrial land uses versus more residential," Tapanes Llahues said. Localities could also shift ad valorem taxes, a challengeable tax based on the assessed value of a property, toward special assessment fees that are based on physical characteristics like square footage or unit count, Mau said. “What we're concerned with is those items being shifted over to the non-ad valorem, and then the property owner has really no way of contesting,” Mau said. DeSantis has tried to take away avenues for localities to raise taxes to compensate for the raised homestead exemption, including passing a law in June that requires a two-thirds vote from local officials to exceed the rollback rate — roughly the same revenue generated from existing properties as the previous year. The larger the proposed increase in the millage rate, the higher the approval threshold. The governor, who will be replaced by fellow Republican Byron Donalds next

items.title: New Northeast Philly Warehouse Sells For $32M: The Philadelphia Deal Sheet
items.description: A construction materials manufacturer has shelled out $32M for a newly built 103K SF warehouse it will use as a distribution center. Courtesy of Crow Holdings 2748 Grant Ave. Crow Holdings Development sold the 10-acre property across from the Northeast Philadelphia Airport to Spears Manufacturing, which produces plastic pipe fittings and valves. “The rapid sale of 2748 Grant Avenue following delivery, along with the significant interest it generated, underscores pent-up demand for modern, Class A warehouse space in a market where new construction remains limited,” CHD Director Johanna Chervak said in a statement. “For industrial owner-users, finding quality, ‘close-in’ properties available for purchase can be challenging.” The property features 32-foot clear heights, 32 loading dock doors and enough parking for 99 vehicles. A CBRE team including Paul Touhey, Sean Bleiler and James Bolt represented the buyer, while JLL's Jeff Lockard, Larry Maister and Mitch Russell represented the seller. SALES Brennan Investment Group purchased a 100K SF warehouse outside Bethlehem at 47 Commerce Way. The acquisition from the nonprofit Feed the Children came out to $11.5M, according to property records. *** Realterm bought a 7-acre final-mile warehouse and industrial outdoor storage fleet maintenance facility at 461 Harrisport Court in Middletown, south of Harrisburg. It includes a 33K SF warehouse and a 6K SF maintenance shop. Realterm declined to share a sale price. The property was sold to UGI Utilities for $775K in 2022, according to property records. Jennifer Stein of JDS Real Estate Services and an Axiom Capital Advisors team including Jose Sasson-Lerner and Roberto Susi helped facilitate the transaction. *** Courtesy of Post Road Management 303–309 N. 65th St. Post Road Management has acquired two West Philadelphia properties spanning 48 units for a combined $1.35M and plans to renovate both properties. The new additions to its portfolio are 303-309 N. 65th St. and 6522-6526 W. Girard Ave., both of which had been foreclosed on. CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT J.G. Petrucci Co. and Mediplex Property Group are working to bring 100K SF of healthcare and retail space to a 15-acre site at 1300 Easton Road in Horsham. Work on the parcel across from the former Willow Grove Naval Air Station is scheduled to begin in the first quarter. *** Shadowbrook Development has received permission from municipal officials in Cinnaminson to build a 45K SF flex warehouse at 2203-2205 Wallace Blvd. The decision was rendered at a meeting Thursday night. PEOPLE Multifamily owner Arden Residential has added two new people to its roster. Brian Collins has joined as president, and Max Spencer has been tapped as managing director of acquisitions and development. THIS AND THAT The Philadelphia Housing Authority and the Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council are offering a reward of up to $30K for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the people who shot and injured a PHA employee at the Morton Homes in East Germantown on Saturday. “This was a senseless and cowardly act of violence against a dedicated public servant who comes to work every day to make our communities a better place to live,” PHA CEO Kelvin Jeremiah said in a statement. “An attack on any member of the PHA family is an attack on all of us, and on the residents we serve. We will not tolerate it.” Anyone with information is encouraged to call the Citizens Crime Commission at 215-546-6532 or the PHA Police Department at 215-684-1911. Anonymous tips may be given by calling 215-684-3350 or emailing Phacrimetips@pha.phila.gov . items.title: 725 Houston Apartments Sit Vacant As Fercan Kalkan Fights Foreclosure
items.description: Despite a mounting debt crisis jeopardizing its $1B portfolio, Houston-based multifamily investment firm Kalkan Capital is still clinging to a troubled, 881-unit housing complex following another attempt by its lender to foreclose. Google Maps The entrance to Rockridge Apartments, a mostly vacant apartment complex in North Houston Filings in a Harris County lawsuit show founder Fercan Kalkan objected to an Oct. 7 notice of a foreclosure sale of the property in Houston’s Greenspoint area, arguing the lenders failed to request the court’s permission. The auction, scheduled for earlier this month, didn’t proceed as the legal battle continues, according to court records. Meanwhile, Rockridge Apartments at 16818 City View Place in North Houston sits 82% vacant, and its conditions are allegedly deteriorating as its owner has gone bankrupt and sought to delay a takeover for more than a year. Kalkan, who previously spoke about his aim to revitalize high-crime communities, didn’t respond to a request for comment. An attorney listed as representing his companies in the Harris County lawsuit said he no longer represents Kalkan-related entities and declined to comment further. Rockridge2016 LLC, a Kalkan affiliate, allegedly defaulted on a $54M loan tied to the property in October 2023, according to legal filings. Computershare Trust Co. sued the LLC in February 2025, requesting the appointment of a receiver and the scheduling of a foreclosure sale. That request was granted, but not before Rockridge2016 filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on April 14, 2025, a move that effectively halts foreclosure proceedings. “I think Dr. Kalkan is trying to avoid your honor’s court, if I’m being candid here,” Ross Travis of the Office of the U.S. Trustee said during a September 2025 bankruptcy hearing, according to audio reviewed by Bisnow . “The more that I see of these cases, the more perplexed I am in general,” Travis said. Despite a court-appointed receiver being in place to manage the complex since August 2025, the complex has “numerous units out of service due to roof, electrical, plumbing, foundation, fire or mold issues,” according to a receivership report filed Friday. Only 156 units are occupied, leaving 725 vacant. Occupancy was marginally higher, at 19%, in August as move-outs outpaced move-ins and raids by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at the property were impacting residents, according to special servicer commentary in the Morningstar Credit database. The Rockridge bankruptcy case was dismissed in December 2025 and officially closed in September. It wasn’t the first time Kalkan has averted foreclosure through legal maneuvers and bankruptcy filings . In early October, the same day the lenders filed a public notice for Rockridge Apartments to be sold at a Nov. 3 foreclosure auction, Kalkan filed his objection in the Harris County lawsuit. Attorneys for the lenders responded the next day, saying that as loan guarantor, Kalkan lacks standing to challenge the foreclosure sale and court authorization isn't required to post the sale notice. The latest property records show the last transfer of ownership for the property is still when Rockridge2016 acquired it in 2016. District Court Judge Dawn Rogers hasn't yet acted on any of the October filings. The next hearing in the case is set for Dec. 9. The attorney representing Computershare Trust Co. and LNR Partners , the loan's special servicer, didn't respond to a request for comment. Kalkan-associated LLCs that owned eight Houston-area properties totaling more than 3,000 units faced potential foreclosure in July 2025. At least six of those properties have been transferred to new owners since, according to property records. items.title: Data centers are paying about 4x what homebuilders pay for comparable land, finds Acres.com CEO Carter Malloy
items.description: At ResiDay 2026 in New York City on Friday, November 6, ResiClub spoke with Carter Malloy , CEO of Acres.com , to talk about a new competitor for land: AI data centers. Acres.com started as a land acquisition business. It closed about 150 deals across the country before turning its in-house tools into a land data platform. Its customers now include large builders such as Lennar, Toll Brothers, and Century Communities, as well as data center developers. One thing the platform does is track land purchases, including buys made through shell companies and outside attorneys, so users can see who is actually buying in a given market. Here's what that data shows, according to Malloy : Data centers aren't everywhere builders are. They're active in only about 10% of the markets where homebuilders operate. But where they're active, they pay far more. On average, data centers are paying about 4x what builders pay for comparable land. For powered land, the gap widens to 10x, 15x, even 20x. Malloy pointed to Central Ohio, where he said the premium is 10x or more across the whole region. The bigger problem is seller expectations. "The problem for us as builders is not, oh, I lost that one parcel," Malloy said. Landowners already had high asking prices, and when a data center moves into the area, they push prices even higher. Malloy called it "an acute problem, not a broad one." Builders don't need to bid on the same parcel as a data center to feel it. If a data center is going up nearby, land costs more, and homes are harder to sell when buyers know there will be a "24/7” noise down the street. Malloy said local governments are pushing back on data centers more and more. Acres' tracking counts more than 400 local data center moratoriums, and he said even that number is low. His bigger worry for builders is where that pushback goes next. Acres' data also shows moratoriums on residential development, multifamily housing, and subdivisions. Once a city council finds out it can stop one kind of development, Malloy said, it may be more willing to stop others. "That is a thing that we are all going to face, I believe, more in the coming year than we have yet." On technology, Malloy said the most innovative builders are doing much more than chatting with ChatGPT. Some, like Lennar and Toll Brothers, have set up in-house development teams that build their own AI tools and connect them to their CRM and ERP systems. Put one person in charge of evaluating AI tools. There are a lot more vendors now. Put a formal AI governance policy in writing, and ask vendors for zero data retention (ZDR) agreements. These are legal promises that your data won't be stored or used to train models.

items.title: Foreclosure filings keep inching up—and are now just a hair below pre-pandemic 2019 levels
items.description: Today’s letter is brought to you by Lennar Investor Marketplace ! Great investment homes can be found all over the country. One of the smartest SFR investment strategies is to diversify your portfolio with properties in a variety of markets. Lennar Investor Marketplace makes it easy with access to homes in 90+ markets—all in one place. With real-time rental comps and local insights like demographics, growth rates and school scores included with every listing, you can find the right mix of investment homes to match your budget, income goals and risk tolerance. Join at no cost to start browsing 2,000+ curated new homes, plus a comprehensive suite of tools and services, including a dedicated Marketplace Concierge. You can even submit your offers right inside the platform with concierge support along the way. Each home features upgrades at no extra cost and a built-in warranty for long-term value and peace of mind. Sign up today to see what’s out there. This month, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York published its quarterly Household Debt and Credit Report. For today’s ResiClub article, we visualized the data and took a closer look at credit and housing distress. U.S. housing foreclosures , by Q3👇 When COVID-19 lockdowns began, the federal government implemented a nationwide foreclosure moratorium to protect homeowners from the economic fallout. These protections—including forbearance programs—were extended multiple times. At the same time, a historic surge in housing demand pushed home prices to new highs during the Pandemic Housing Boom, boosting homeowner equity and keeping foreclosure activity unusually low. But in recent quarters, foreclosures have steadily returned, inching closer to pre-pandemic 2019 levels. The question heading forward: Will housing foreclosures be higher in 2027? Based on delinquency data alone, U.S. foreclosures are likely to tick up a little over the next 12 months. Of course, if the macro environment were to shift and a recession were to materialize, that trajectory could change. But as of now, if all else remains constant, the current path points to a gradual increase. Before U.S. housing foreclosures rise, 90+ day mortgage delinquencies typically increase. While 90+ day credit card and auto delinquencies have surged to levels seen during the Great Financial Crisis, 90+ day mortgage delinquencies have only recently surpassed pre-pandemic 2019 levels. Percent of household mortgage balances 90+ days delinquent , by Q3👇 On the 90+ days delinquency front, the most noticeable development is that student loan delinquencies surged last year. While the jump was expected after years of artificially low student loan delinquency rates, Fed researchers warned of serious consequences for behind student loan borrowers, including damaged credit and reduced access to mortgages and auto loans. According to the New York Fed , superprime U.S. borrowers—those with credit scores above 760—who carry unpaid student loan balances saw their credit scores drop by an average of 171 points in mid-2025. That’s because student loan delinquencies, which hadn’t been reported to credit bureaus since the start of the pandemic, started being reported again last year. This sudden credit hit may have temporarily pushed some borrowers out of the housing market in 2026. The Treasury has also resumed collection tactics on student loans, including wage garnishment and tax refund seizures, raising questions about potential spillover into other areas of consumer credit. And before 90+ day delinquencies typically increase, 30+ day delinquencies usually rise first. Indeed, 30+ day mortgage delinquencies have returned to pre-pandemic 2019 levels. Percent of household mortgages transitioning into 30+ days delinquent , by Q3👇 Looking through a historical lens, mortgage delinquencies are still fairly low right now. That said, FHA mortgages—which are backed by the Federal Housing Administration and often used by first-time or lower-income homebuyers—have seen a notable spike in delinquencies over the past two years. We should continue to keep an eye on that. In a report published earlier this year, the New York Fed finds that the recent rise in mortgage delinquencies has been greatest in lower-income ZIP codes. Keep in mind that FHA mortgages make up a much smaller share of overall borrowers than, say, GSE conventional borrowers (guaranteed by Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac). According to the New York Fed, in 2025, FHA mortgages represent just 12% of the nation’s outstanding mortgage debt. The U.S. South—the epicenter of U.S. single-family homebuilding—has a greater concentration of FHA mortgages. Big picture: While U.S. housing foreclosures remain low and below pre-pandemic 2019 levels, the 30+ days delinquency data suggest that foreclosures could gradually near pre-pandemic 2019 in the near future. If that trend accelerates or shifts, we’ll be sure to keep you informed.

items.title: Inside a 3-Home Co-Living Compound Designed for Friends To Buy Together
items.description: A co-living community in West Oakland, CA , has hit the market for the first time. The Union is a three-house, 14-bedroom compound and is listed at $2,999,995. That’s the asking price for all three homes. If purchased separately by friends, multigenerational families, or any other buyers who want to live side by side, the starting price is $899,000 for the smallest of the three homes, which has five bedrooms and four bathrooms . Each home is separately deeded as a condo within the greater compound. This lot has been zoned RM-3, or Mixed Housing Type Residential–3, which allows for multiple single-family homes on a single lot. This setup is permissible due to changes in California law allowing for higher-density housing in residential areas. Loading... The Union was built as a three-home, 14-bedroom co-living compound. Aerial Canvas Loading... The design matches the existing look and feel of the neighborhood, which is filled with mostly Victorian homes. Aerial Canvas Loading... The shared rooftop deck boasts views of downtown Oakland. Aerial Canvas This project started in 2019 when a startup called Open Door bought the 7,535-square-foot empty lot and tasked Matt Baran of Baran Studio Architecture with creating a co-living space. They asked: “What if we design something that can be beautiful design and work with the new state laws that allow for increased density in neighborhoods and works well for community living?” says listing agent Max Nelson , who specializes in co-living sales through the platform Live Near Friends . The end result was a rent-by-the-room community where residents enjoyed shared amenities, including a backyard fire pit, co-working space, and rooftop deck with views of downtown Oakland. The design process balanced group-friendly amenities with the look and feel of the neighborhood, which is filled with mostly Victorian homes. Nelson says that the architects asked, “How do we create a modern house without making it look like it doesn't fit?” The design included bay windows that jut from the homes, mirroring the style of a classic Victorian. Having three separate homes rather than one huge building also matched the aesthetic of the area, as did the incorporation of tall, narrow windows. Much of the rest of the design leans more modern, especially the efficient energy systems. The homes rely on shared solar panels, greatly reducing energy bills. Everything is electric—there is no reliance on gas. Each room has its own fan coils to create customized comfort. “It’s a super efficient, well-done system,” says Nelson. Loading... The appliances in the kitchen are electric. Aerial Canvas Loading... The design included bay windows that jut from the homes, mirroring the style of a classic Victorian. Aerial Canvas Because The Union was designed for co-living, some of the best features are the shared spaces and the flow among the three homes. The property fronting the street, 1514, has the smaller price tag at $899,000 and offers 1,919 square feet of living space, including five bedrooms and four bathrooms. A skybridge connects it with the back two condos, positioned side by side like a duplex and sharing a common wall. The larger of the back condos, 1510, is listed at $1,049,500 and sits slightly larger at 2,033 square feet, again with five bedrooms and four bathrooms. Connected is 1512, also offered at $1,049,500 with 2,015 square feet, including four bedrooms and four bathrooms. Above these two condos is the roof area, which houses the solar panels as well as the communal deck with AstroTurf and several seating areas. It all adds up to a highly functional, thoughtfully designed compound that meets the needs of communal living. It offers both shared spaces as well as smaller decks, outdoor seating nooks, and private spaces for solo or one-on-one time with another—because shared living works best when people have the freedom to come together or enjoy time apart. items.title: How the Kennedys Spent Thanksgiving at Their Hyannis Port Compound—Where JFK and His Father Plotted a Presidential Run
items.description: When John F. Kennedy came home to Hyannis Port for his first Thanksgiving as president, his father still had the best seat in the house. Joseph P. Kennedy presided over the family table, the children ate first, and the cranberries served with dinner came from bogs near the family’s Cape Cod retreat. Five years earlier, it was what happened after Thanksgiving dinner that the family would remember. John, then a Massachusetts senator, slipped into the study off the living room with his father. He had a list of reasons to think twice about running for president. Joseph had an answer for every one. By the time they emerged, the Kennedys had a campaign to plan . Loading... When John F. Kennedy came home to Hyannis Port for his first Thanksgiving as president, his father still had the best seat in the house. Hy Peskin/Getty Images Thanksgiving at the Big House The house where that conversation took place began as a summer rental. In 1926, Joseph and his wife, Rose , brought their children to Malcolm Cottage, a waterfront home overlooking Nantucket Sound. John was just 9. According to the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum, Joseph bought the property two years later for $25,000 and expanded the house to accommodate his growing family. John eventually bought a place of his own behind his parents’ home. His brother Robert and sister-in-law Ethel came to own an adjoining property. Together, the three residences formed the 6-acre compound, an arrangement that put several generations of Kennedys within walking distance of Thanksgiving dinner at the Big House. In "White House by the Sea," author Kate Storey describes a family with surprisingly little use for a formal seating plan. Joseph and Rose took opposite ends of the mahogany table. Everyone else picked a spot. Family cook Ziptha Anderson remembered far less flexibility when it came to carving the bird. “They all like the same thing—the white meat,” she said. The weather had a say in the menu, too. A chilly Thanksgiving called for clam broth, while a mild afternoon meant tomato juice to start. Dinner was at 1 p.m. in Storey’s account of the 1956 gathering, which still left the family time for Mass and a sail before they made their way to the table. A president comes home for the holiday Loading... By Thanksgiving 1961, the guest list included 13 Kennedy adults and 15 Kennedy children. There was room for another family, too. Paul Fay, then undersecretary of the Navy, joined the celebration with his wife and their three children. CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images By Thanksgiving 1961, the guest list included 13 Kennedy adults and 15 Kennedy children. There was room for another family, too. Paul Fay , then undersecretary of the Navy, joined the celebration with his wife and their three children. One family outing took the president and several of his siblings to the skating rink in Hyannis named for their late brother, Joseph Jr. John watched while Ted and his sisters rented skates and played tag on the ice. Back at the compound, Bobby and Ted also got a touch football game going. That evening, the adults sat down to Vermont turkey, candied sweet potatoes, and their choice of pies. Ted found another way to work up an appetite in 1979. A United Press International photographer caught the senator waving from his boat as he took relatives and friends sailing off Hyannis Port before Thanksgiving dinner. Loading... For nearly a century, the Kennedy family's sprawling Hyannis Port compound has served as the backdrop to countless summer celebrations, where days were spent sailing on Nantucket Sound, swimming off the Cape Cod coastline, and taking part in fiercely competitive games of touch football. Instagram / Kerry Kennedy The year the turkey got away Ethel carried on hosting Thanksgiving at Hyannis Port long after her children had families of their own. In 2010, she enlisted her son Robert to bring home two live turkeys so her grandchildren could see the birds up close. One promptly escaped. “For three days they chased it everywhere,” Ethel told the Cape Cod Times. A couple of months later, the newspaper ran a story about a turkey causing trouble in nearby Centerville, where it had even taken on a moving postal truck. Ethel called the newsroom. She thought she knew where the bird had come from. Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

items.title: Thanksgiving Murder Mystery Remains Unsolved 30 Years After Killer Allegedly Used Cat Door to Enter Woman’s Texas Apartment
items.description: For 30 years, Thanksgiving has been a painful reminder for a Texas family whose holiday turned into a nightmare when their loved one was found strangled inside her Houston apartment. Kristen Lea Wilson , 29, was preparing to spend Thanksgiving with her family in November 1996 when investigators say someone slipped into her first-floor apartment through a window, using a cat door to gain access, and waited for her to return home. After cutting the telephone cord and unscrewing the lightbulbs to keep the apartment dark, the intruder waited in Wilson’s bedroom closet. When she never showed up to Thanksgiving dinner the following day, her parents became worried and drove her apartment where they found her slain body. Three decades later, no one has been charged in her murder , and her family is still fighting for answers. “Thirty years ago this Thanksgiving my sister Kristen Lea Wilson was murdered in Houston,” Kelly Wilson Hancock wrote in a recent social media post. “She was strangled–this was an up and personal murder. Her case has NEVER been solved.” A killer waiting inside On Nov. 27, 1996, the day before Thanksgiving, Wilson stopped at a grocery store after work to pick up last-minute items for the family's holiday gathering at her grandparents' home in Katy, TX. She returned to her apartment on Meadowglen Lane in southwest Houston, unloaded her groceries, and reportedly went into her bedroom to change clothes. Investigators believe her killer was already inside. According to the Houston Police Department, the intruder likely gained access by reaching through a cat door in the screen of a first-floor window and removing the window frame. Once inside, the killer allegedly cut the telephone cord and unscrewed lightbulbs, reportedly preparing to ambush Wilson in complete darkness. The apartment's accessibility became a crucial detail in the investigation, and raised troubling questions about security at the complex, especially because Wilson had allegedly expressed concerns about her safety before her death, her family said. She had previously revealed an incident in which a maintenance worker allegedly entered her apartment without warning. Loading... Kristen Wilson was killed inside her apartment on Meadowglen Lane in southwest Houston, after arriving home the day before Thanksgiving. Investigators believe her killer was already inside. Google Maps When Wilson’s parents arrived at her apartment to check on her, they found the front door unlocked. Inside, Wilson's father made the horrific discovery–his daughter dead on the bedroom floor. She had been strangled and was partially undressed. Police also noted a disturbing detail–her body appeared to have been deliberately positioned, with her ankles crossed and her hands resting in her lap. Investigators found evidence of a violent struggle, including broken fingernails, suggesting Wilson had fought desperately against her attacker. There were no reported witnesses to the killing, and surveillance cameras did not capture the suspect leaving the property. Could new DNA technology finally solve the case? Despite decades of investigation, extensive media coverage and advancements in forensic technologies, the identity of Wilson’s killer remains a mystery. Three men associated with Wilson provided DNA samples to investigators shortly after her death, and each were ruled out as suspects based on the technology available at the time, according to an investigation by ABC13 Houston . But Hancock believes mistakes made during the initial investigation have complicated efforts to solve her sister's murder. “From the get go, the detectives messed up,” she wrote in her recent post. “The original detective was going through a divorce and she wasn’t focused.” She also expressed frustration over what she described as inconsistencies in the investigation. Investigators have since discovered that not all the evidence collected from the crime scene was tested, according to local reports. Hancock said she has attempted to contact Othram, a forensic DNA laboratory that specializes in helping law enforcement investigate cold cases, about potentially examining evidence in her sister's murder. “I’ve tried to reach out to Othram Labs to see if they can look at DNA, but the detective has to request it, from what I am told,” she wrote. It is unclear whether Houston police have submitted evidence for additional testing or whether forensic genetic genealogy could be used in the case. Loading... Despite decades of investigation, extensive media coverage and advancements in forensic technologies, the identity of Kristen Wilson’s killer remains a mystery. Texas Department of Public Safety A family’s Thanksgiving nightmare For the Wilson family, Thanksgiving had always been one of their favorite celebrations. “Thanksgiving was the biggest event of the year,” Hancock told ABC13 . “We’d all go over there, and it was just a big family get-together. It was so much fun.” Wilson, described by her sister as independent and ambitious, had launched a small business that provided office services to local companies. Wilson, the middle of three girls, was also devoted to her family, especially her young niece and nephew. "She was like a second mother to my son and daughter,” Hancock said. “She was just so beautiful with an infectious smile. My mom always called her the golden child because she just was. I hate to say she was perfect, but she pretty much was.”. The Wilson family was devastated by her murder and to this day are still struggling with questions that remain unanswered three decades later. “My grandma used the words ‘brutally murdered.’ I’ll never forget the call telling me Kristen had been killed," Hancock said. "My whole world was… our whole family’s world was turned upside down. Personally, I think she knew the person, but I don’t know." items.title: The Bottom of the Bottom? (November 2026 Housing Market Forecast)
items.description: The Bottom of the Bottom? (November 2026 Housing Market Forecast) Written by Mischa Fisher on November 25, 2026 The shift in strength from the for-sale market to the rental market that we highlighted earlier in the year continues to pick up momentum. The rate of decline has become large enough that Zillow’s latest forecast predicts home sales for full-year 2026 will decline slightly, while home values will have risen only modestly in nominal terms (i.e., home values rising slower than the rate of inflation). Home values are projected to rise 0.4% this year, revised down from 0.7% last month, driven mainly by the run-up in inventory. Mortgage rates hit 7.3% in October and could stay above 7% through mid-2027, which will keep many buyers on the sidelines while listings pile up. Despite new listings slowing year over year, total active listings could be as much as 10% higher than last year by December. Because the labor market is marked by low hiring and low firing, widespread job loss has been avoided, and that has held up best where supply is still tight, in the Central and Northeast regions. The West, with more inventory growth, faces more downward pressure on prices despite the relatively low unemployment rate. Existing home sales are now projected to reach 3.71 million in 2026, down from last month’s estimate of 3.75 million. This means that despite the stronger months during higher-volume portions of the year, the acute slowdown in the lower-volume fourth quarter is putting enough downward pressure on existing home sales that 2026 will finish with slightly fewer home sales than 2025 (but still 2.2% more than 2024). Zillow’s forecast of existing home sales, as measured by NAR, is expected to fall 1.4% to 4.0 million. Zillow projects single-family rents will rise 2.9% in 2026, while multifamily rents are expected to grow 1.8%. The rent forecast was adjusted upward because elevated rates and affordability pressure are pushing more would-be buyers to keep renting. Rent growth is still below historical norms. The Bottom of the bottom? All markets are cyclical, and in time, this too shall pass. But this existing and forecasted acute decline in sales activity, from an already low baseline, does prompt the question: where is the bottom of the bottom? The answer depends in part on which metric we use to define the bottom, and so it is susceptible to shifting with timing, level of aggregation, and seasonal adjustment. For example, Zillow’s existing home sales metric is calculated by counting the complete actuals of sales transactions and comparing those totals to the prior year. This is different method from NAR’s existing sales process, which is based on regional samples and converted into a seasonally adjusted annual rate. Practically, this means the low point of the two methods can differ, and NAR’s could be affected by any drift in regional mix that isn’t picked up by the sampling. But for now, if we define the bottom of the bottom as the peak rate of decline in existing sales from a low baseline level, I think October and November of 2026 have a high likelihood of being the bottom of the post-COVID years. Even though timing the total level of low sales is sensitive to how the trend annualizes, it stands to reason that these months may also represent the lowest total sales volume of the post-COVID era, regardless of whether or not one measures using NAR’s sampled, seasonally adjusted annual rate or Zillow’s full count of transactions. Less volatility, lower inflation, a slowdown in debt issuance to hyperscalers, and the unwinding of some of the global conflicts could all contribute to lower treasuries, lower yield spreads, and higher home sales in the final third of the 2020s.
